name: CAGE Questionnaire
construct: Lifetime screen for problem drinking through 4 questions: cut down, annoyed, guilty, eye opener.
licence: "Believed to be in the public domain" (CamCOPS, citing Mayfield et al. 1974, Ewing 1984 and O'Brien 2008; Ewing 1984, the original author, encourages widespread use).
instructions: Ask your patients these four questions and use the scoring method described below to determine if substance abuse exists and needs to be addressed.

items.text: Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?
Have people annoyed you by criticizing your drinking?
Have you ever felt bad or guilty about your drinking?
Have you ever had a drink first thing in the morning to steady your nerves or to get rid of a hangover (eye-opener)?

scoring: Score each item 0 for no and 1 for yes and sum (0 to 4); higher scores indicate greater likelihood of alcohol problems. A total of 2 or more is considered clinically significant (Ewing, 1984); the SAMHSA Consensus Panel recommends primary care clinicians lower the threshold to 1 positive answer to identify more patients. The CAGE-AID adapts the items to include drug use.
citation: Ewing, J. A. (1984). Detecting alcoholism: The CAGE questionnaire. JAMA, 252(14), 1905-1907. https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.1984.03350140051025
transcriptionNote: The CamCOPS page (itemsUrl) gives the citations and public domain statement but not the question text. The items were transcribed from the SCIRE Project CAGE Substance Screening Tool PDF, which cites Ewing (1984) as source and prints the clinician instruction above; a second open copy (University of Washington, https://depts.washington.edu/edgh/zw/vl/project-resources/CAGE_Questionnaire.pdf) differs in wording for items 1, 3 and 4 ("felt you needed to Cut down", "felt Guilty about drinking", "felt you needed a drink first thing in the morning (Eye-opener) to steady your nerves or to get rid of a hangover?"). The SCIRE wording, which matches the Ewing (1984) JAMA wording, is used. The instruction recorded is the clinician instruction from the SCIRE form; there is no standard respondent instruction. US spelling (criticizing) retained.
